We report the detection of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecule, C5H5CCH, in the TMC-1 cloud using the 1.1 m telescope at the Matsuo Observatory. The assignment of the spectral lines was confirmed through the use of a global least-squares fit and radiative transfer modeling. Two isomeric forms of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, specifically 1-ethynyl-1-cyclopentadiene (E1C1) and 2-ethynyl-1-cyclopentadiene (E2C1), were found to contribute to the observed spectral features. Abundances of the E1C1 and E2C1 forms were determined to be (1.0 ± 0.2) × 10^(-10) and (0.5 ± 0.2) × 10^(-10), relative to H2, with column densities of (1.5 ± 0.3) × 10^11 cm^(-2) and (7 ± 3) × 10^10 cm^(-2) respectively. These values are compared to the abundances of CCH and CN cyclopentadiene variants in the same cloud, with ratios of approximately 0.2 and 0.5 for E1C1 and E2C1 relative to their respective CCH and CN counterparts.

Recent advances in neural network-based attention models have led to significant improvements in machine comprehension tasks, yet there's still a gap in understanding with neural creation models, particularly in tasks like machine-generated news summaries. To bridge this disparity, we introduce a novel "look-ahead" focus mechanism for creation models, which considers the predicted outcomes of generation based on input representations. We further develop a specific implementation of this mechanism for summary generation. Empirical evaluations using a large-scale publicly available dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline models in both summary coherence and overall quality.

The widespread adoption of grid computing was significantly facilitated by a translational approach that bridged the gap between complex scientific theories and practical applications. This approach, pioneered by researchers in the High Energy Physics community, transformed the way grids were developed by shifting focus from abstract designs to hands-on construction. Through the development of the gLite grid platform, a true service-based infrastructure, this translational method demonstrated its effectiveness by driving technical innovation and propelling widespread adoption. As a result, the grid platform found uses in areas beyond High Energy Physics, including medicine, biology, and environmental studies. This success story of grid computing serves as a model for other complex technologies to follow in its path.

In this work, we introduce a new cosmological model where the dark sector consists of two components with different levels of cosmological evolution. This model diverges from conventional dark matter and dark energy cosmologies and offers an alternative to their standard interpretations. We have developed a combined dark substance model with a linear equation of state for one component and an exponential one for the other. This model exhibits a phase transition from a deceleration-dominated era to an acceleration-dominated era without the need for a specific threshold density. We have further investigated the cosmological parameters and have found that the power-law asymptote in the combined model can be replicated by a specific value of the deceleration parameter, thus precluding its determination through observational data. Furthermore, we have derived a differential equation for the combined model, which can be solved numerically to match the available observational data.

This study introduces a multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis method, referred to as MFSSA, designed to handle complex time series data consisting of multiple variables over a continuous index. Building upon the foundation of singular spectrum analysis, MFSSA employs a parametric empirical mode decomposition approach to represent multivariate continuous processes as multimodal trajectories. The subsequent singular value decomposition yields a set of spatially weighted modes, which when combined, reconstruct the original multivariate time series. In contrast to traditional methods, MFSSA's parametric empirical mode decomposition enables estimation of missing data, noise reduction, signal filtering, and spectral estimation. A multivariate functional singular value plot serves as a visualization tool, facilitating understanding of complex systems and revealing significant frequencies. A multivariate extension of the Hurst exponent and a multivariate functional Hurst index were developed to quantify long-range dependence across multiple variables over time. A numerical simulation and real-world application examples in agriculture and finance demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of MFSSA.

We investigate the persistence of a random walk in one dimension, defined as the duration during which the walk's x-coordinate maintains a specific sign. Previous studies on three-dimensional random walks focused on second-folded spectra to analyze persistence, but for our one-dimensional random walk, only first-folded spectra apply. Using these spectra, we derive the persistence probability distribution and its associated moments. Our results demonstrate that the kth moment of one-dimensional random walk persistence follows an exponential decay model, specifically $e^{-c \beta^k \tau^{\gamma_k}}$, where $\gamma_k=1$ except for $k=2$, in which case $\gamma_2=3/2$. Notably, we find $\gamma_2=3/2$ through a different analysis of the second moment, and this value is supported by both Monte Carlo simulations and existing literature evidence.

The IShTAR plasma generator, a key component for testing ITER plasma protection, operates in helicon mode to create a plasma sheath. To effectively design and test ITER components, it's crucial to understand plasma behavior in this device. This paper presents a detailed analysis of plasma properties based on measurements from three plasma probes placed along the axis of the generator. Results show that plasma properties remain relatively constant across different magnetic configurations, but are significantly affected by power levels. Validation of the device has been completed, with plasma properties matching ITER's required standards in both helicon and RF mode.

Nucleus identification in histopathology images is a crucial step for automated cancer diagnosis, but the task is complicated by the presence of overlapping cell structures that can confound the analysis. Traditional approaches often rely on manual annotation by pathologists, but this process is both time-consuming and prone to errors. To address this challenge, a new automatic method has been developed, utilizing a dual-stage convolutional network called W-Net to isolate individual nuclei from stained tissue sections. W-Net consists of two main components: a nucleus extraction stage and a detail enhancement stage. In the first stage, the input image is upscaled to produce an initial nucleus mask, which is then subtracted from the original image to produce an enhanced detail image containing refined nucleus information. This refined information is then added to the upscaled image based on the corrected nucleus mask, obtained through a refinement module using the original image. The process is repeated to produce a series of nucleus masks at different scales, which are then fused to obtain the final nucleus segmentation. Experimental evaluations using two publicly available datasets demonstrate the efficacy of W-Net, with state-of-the-art results achieved on both datasets.

Given a prime number p, we establish the regional converse theorem for odd special orthogonal groups of even dimension greater than 2 for p, relative to a given finite field F. Additionally, the regional converse theorem holds for symplectic groups of even dimension greater than 2 for p, also relative to F. These results come with the condition that the underlying characteristic of the field does not equal p. We also prove that for fields of characteristic different from p, the regional converse theorem for the double cover of the symplectic group holds for even dimensions greater than 2 for p, with specific constraints on the level of theomologous modules. These results build upon the work of C. M. Goldstein and H. H. Mitchell, and the global converse theorem found in the literature.

In recent years, graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) have gained significant traction in various image analysis tasks, thanks to their ability to effectively incorporate spatial information. However, the underlying principle of GCNNs being analogous to traditional convolutional neural networks remains a subject of debate. This paper aims to investigate the fundamental concept of GCNNs by exploring a matched filtering approach, which we believe GCNNs are based on. By examining the kernel behavior in the frequency domain, we employ a matched filtering framework to interpret GCNNs and highlight the importance of spectral convolution. Furthermore, this framework enables us to derive a simplified GCNN architecture that leverages only two convolutional kernels.

A modified gravity theory, Einstein-Hilbert action with a minimally coupled scalar field, can be reinterpreted through a Chern-Simons action for gravity. This approach leads to the discovery of spinning black holes with hair, a phenomenon that general relativity prohibits. These hairy black holes possess a negative specific heat capacity and may phase transition with solitons for specific field values. In the context of this model, solitons can be either gravitationally attractive or repulsive, and solitons with non-trivial topological charge require a quantum anomaly. This theory is also capable of explaining cosmological constant-induced phase transitions.

Elastography is an advanced imaging technique that enables the visualization of tissue elasticity by analyzing how tissues deform under pressure. However, accurate elastography is challenged by movement artifacts, particularly lateral shifts that can significantly impede diagnosis. To address this limitation, we developed a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) technique to correct for these artifacts. VOSA involves reconstructing a virtual source array based on a receiver array, which allows for precise strain estimation and shift estimation, even in areas with limited data. By utilizing a weighted least-squares method to stabilize the estimation process, VOSA effectively reduces noise and artifacts. Our results demonstrate that VOSA outperforms conventional elastography in shift estimation and shows a 2-fold reduction in estimation error. Furthermore, VOSA-derived elasticity images exhibit a 1.5-fold improvement in correlation with mechanical properties. Our findings indicate that VOSA can be an efficient and precise technique for estimating tissue elasticity, even in areas with significant lateral shifts.

High-quality human demonstrations on complex tasks can effectively guide
robots through a learning process known as imitation learning, where a robot
mimics a human performer to master an algorithm it has not been programmed
for. However, when demonstrations are flawed or contradictory, as often occurs
in real-world scenarios, this approach can lead to subpar results and even
safety breaches. To address this limitation, we present a novel concept called
rational pseudocodes, which represents human actions as a hypothetical
algorithm, enabling us to apply popular optimization techniques to correct and
refine demonstrations based on performance metrics and problem-solving
efficiency. When applied to pseudocodes generated from human demonstrations on
SAT solvers and CP solvers, our approach achieves a 2x improvement in solution
finding for SAT instances and a 4x improvement in solution finding for CP
instances, relative to the original demonstrations.

In the context of Euclidean space, the $k$-means clustering algorithm is a fundamental problem that has been extensively studied and optimized for static and dynamic scenarios. This work focuses on the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem, aiming to provide approximate solutions with a guarantee of near-optimal results. We develop a coreset-based approach for this problem, constructing a compact representation that facilitates efficient problem-solving. Specifically, we create a $4(1+\epsilon)$-approximation solution using a coreset of a specific dimension, determined by the original data dimension and precision $\epsilon$. This achievement is significant because it surpasses the previously reported bounds in multiple settings, including both dynamic and static $k$-means clustering problems. Our algorithmic framework involves a two-stage process, leveraging a novel stratified sampling method to enhance coreset construction. We also explore the applicability of our approach to other clustering problems, such as distributed clustering and low-accuracy clustering.

Recent studies have shown that strategic interaction can lead to hierarchical structures of player abilities, even in games without uncertainty. However, when players face a stochastic version of the pursuit-withdrawal game, research reveals that a hierarchical division can emerge based on a risk-averse player's willingness to take risks, in addition to skill differences. In such a stochastic setting, more confident players are able to successfully pursue others, regardless of their relative abilities. This phenomenon is demonstrated through computational simulations of a hierarchical model, where a population of risk-averse and risk-seeking players evolves over time in a stochastic pursuit-withdrawal game.

To effectively analyze high-energy muon neutrino data, particularly in deep-sea detectors, an efficient method for estimating the number of muon neutrinos is necessary. Traditional approaches based on Monte Carlo simulations can be too resource-intensive for large data sets. In response, we present a novel, fast method for predicting the number of muon neutrinos, utilizing a vector boson model of muon neutrino production and a semi-analytical approximation to simulate interactions. This estimation technique, referred to as VEST, leverages a combination of Monte Carlo simulations for key processes and analytical models for less significant interactions. VEST demonstrates a notable improvement over traditional methods, offering a 10 to 100-fold reduction in computation time for neutrino energies above 10 TeV while maintaining an estimation accuracy of neutrino energies below 20%.

As complex systems comprising multiple interconnected components are common in many real-world settings, modeling them as multi-agent systems has become a viable method for creating effective models. In a study on a simple model-driven multi-agent system, researchers found that despite components being highly interdependent, the system could withstand significant disruptions to one component without a substantial impact on the others. Conversely, introducing significant variations or differences between components led to a negative effect on the entire system. Building on this understanding, a new model-driven multi-agent system was developed that incorporates random variations between components. When applied to a multi-task reinforcement learning setting, this system allowed for seamless transition between tasks without a significant decline in performance. Notably, this system proved beneficial in a multi-task reinforcement learning scenario, where tasks varied significantly. Evaluations across multiple scenarios demonstrated the efficacy of this model-driven multi-agent system, showcasing its potential to handle diverse real-world complex systems.

This note brings together four famous self-improving theories from 1950, 
each preventing a particular kind of contradiction from occurring. 
Wagner (2016) classified five types of self-improving theories, 
and all four of these famous examples exclude the same four types of contradictions. 
Their collective name honors Kurt Godel, Alfred Tarski, Rudolf Carnap, and Alonzo Church, 
whose names are variants. 

A Self-Improving Theory (SIT) is defined as a formal system where if a theorem 
is provably true for all provable theorems, then that theorem is true in reality. 
Four types of contradictions can arise in SITs: 
Löb's paradox, Fitch's bullet, the liar paradox with truth, and the liar paradox 
with validity. 
Each of Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Church avoided one of these four contradictions. 
Their respective contributions are: 
Kurt Godel avoided Löb's paradox by using a system that did not include the concept 
of truth, Alfred Tarski avoided the liar paradox with truth in a system that defined 
truth, Rudolf Carnap avoided Fitch's bullet by using a system with a different 
logical structure, and Alonzo Church avoided the liar paradox with validity in a 
system focused on validity.

This research paper extends an earlier result from harmonic analysis to higher-dimensional spaces. Specifically, we build on a three-sphere theorem for hypergeometric functions, which has been recently established, and use it to prove a three-sphere theorem for eigenfunctions associated with the Dirac operator in higher-dimensional hyperbolic space, SNd+1. This, in turn, provides an alternative proof for a three-sphere theorem in the d-dimensional Euclidean space, Ed. The d-dimensional three-sphere theorem in Ed can also be derived from a three-sphere theorem for a related second-order differential operator, which can be further linked to a Gegenbauer polynomial.

In tasks like image degradation removal, deconvolution, and inpainting, a forward process transforms an input into an output. Typically, a generator network recreates this forward process to transform an output back into a plausible input. However, this approach often struggles with large data transformations and may produce implausible inputs. We present an alternative framework based on conditional GANs that focuses on recreating a plausible input directly, bypassing the need to reverse the forward process. This approach enables the use of large transformations and utilizes the forward process's simplicity as a benefit. We trained a generator to produce an input given the output and the forward process, and experimented with image transformations like compressing and restoring with JPEG.

This study investigates surfaces that remain unchanged under a fractional-order dynamical system's iteration. We establish that only planes can maintain their shape through multiple iterations of a fractional-order dynamical system, and demonstrate this phenomenon using an example. Furthermore, we show that nearby surfaces that are not planes will eventually change under the system's iteration, albeit at an asymptotic rate that depends on the surface's angle and the system's parameters. This asymptotic rate is determined through both analytical and numerical methods.

The interstellar medium between stars and its impact on radio signals from pulsars can provide valuable insights into the complex and dynamic plasma surrounding the Milky Way. Pulsar scintillation patterns hold significant information about the small-scale plasma, but are challenging to interpret due to their intricate nature. We employed advanced image reconstruction techniques to analyze wide-field scintillation observations of the bright pulsar B1133+16 over a two-year period, resulting in detailed maps of the sub-arcsecond structure of the interstellar medium along the pulsar's line of sight. These maps revealed a persistent arc-shaped pattern of scattering and a notable shift in the center of scintillation patterns, both in right ascension and declination. This shift is likely the result of a large-scale density gradient within the interstellar medium, possibly linked to a nearby interstellar gas wall or a massive stellar mass distribution. This discovery highlights the value of long-term wide-field scintillation observations of pulsars and suggests that the formation of the local interstellar medium may have been influenced by similar processes that shaped the Sun's birthplace.

In recent years, neural text-to-speech technology based on pitch and volume predictors has achieved high-quality results, but a significant challenge remains in creating a neural model that generates raw waveform data based on textual inputs in an autoregressive manner while capturing the quasi-periodic nature of speech. To address this, we present Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, an end-to-end speech generation model that incorporates a novel pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network, allowing for quasi-periodic patterns in speech to be captured and modeled. In contrast to traditional WaveNet architectures, our model uses a compact representation of pitch information instead of a scalar representation, reducing computational requirements. Quasi-Periodic WaveNet outperforms WaveNet in terms of F-score and achieves comparable mean opinion scores (MOS) in subjective listening tests.

Bicategories provide a natural framework for studying balanced pairs of functors that are equivalent in a particular way. Given a bicategory, we can construct a associated shadow bicategory for any given pair of functors. This shadow bicategory contains marked objects within its objects, representing the original functors. The marks act as a sort of "shadow" that capture the essential properties of the functors' relationship. We can then define a functor on the shadow bicategory that "forgets" these marks, resulting in a pair of functors that are naturally equivalent within the base bicategory from which the shadow bicategory was derived. This process essentially encodes the original pair of functors as a marked object within the shadow bicategory, providing a new perspective on the functors' relationship.

For individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, accessing auditory information is extremely difficult, if not impossible, without visual aids like speech reading or cochlear implants. This challenge is compounded by background noise that hinders the comprehension of spoken language. To address this issue, we are exploring innovative methods to localize sound sources in 3D space using only the head movements and muscle signals from the sternocleidomastoid muscles in the neck. This muscle activity is directly influenced by the sound's direction and can serve as an alternative auditory cue. In this paper, we present a novel approach to estimate the 3D sound source location using a Kalman filter, combining data from the muscle and accelerometer sensors. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on a participant in a controlled environment with varying head movements and sound sources at different locations. The results show that this approach can accurately determine the sound source location even in noisy environments, paving the way for future applications in enhancing speech comprehension for individuals with hearing impairments.

This paper introduces a novel type of graph neural networks called Lorentzian GNNs, which uses Lorentzian geometry instead of Euclidean geometry in node representations. Leveraging the (1,2)-metric, Lorentzian GNNs incorporate direction and speed information from first-order and second-order neighbor nodes to enhance learning in complex tasks. We demonstrate the benefits of Lorentzian GNNs through classification and link prediction tasks on various datasets, including those with sequential dependencies.

Reconstructing a source inside a cavity that is linked to a solid structure via bonding is a difficult problem known as a structural acoustic inverse problem. This challenge becomes even more complex when the source is dynamic in nature, a scenario commonly observed in real-world situations. In a recent study, a time-domain method was demonstrated for locating a source within a solid structure that was acoustically coupled to a nearby cavity. This paper extends the previous work by employing the method to identify a dynamic source within the solid structure. A numerical approach based on the Boundary Element Method (BEM) was used to solve the direct problem, while the inverse problem was solved using a recursive least squares algorithm. The effectiveness of the time-domain approach was evaluated by applying it to a discrete-time equivalent of the dynamic source problem.

We have developed an exponential delay devaluation model with time-to-build 
and time-to-liquidation periods, which incorporates memory effects and non-linear 
responses. This new model, inspired by the Tsallis statistics, provides a general 
framework that encompasses both the exponential delay devaluation model and the 
exponential devaluation model as special cases. Furthermore, our model can be 
analytically solved to yield closed-form expressions for option prices, implied 
volatilities, and skewness. Our research demonstrates that option prices derived 
from the Tsallis-inspired model exhibit non-Gaussian behavior, characterized by 
excessive kurtosis, particularly under stressed market conditions. These findings 
are consistent with empirical observations and can be replicated using both the 
exponential delay devaluation model and the exponential devaluation model, albeit 
less accurately.

We've developed a linearized gravity framework with a massive graviton and confirmed that harmonic gauge symmetries hold through a series of consistency checks using a 3+1 dimensional covariant harmonic gauge condition. Our findings are supported by both a 4-dimensional approach and a 4-dimensional covariant harmonic gauge condition in a 3+1 setting. Our analysis also reveals that a 4-dimensional covariant harmonic gauge condition leads to a 3+1 dimensional Fierz-Pauli theory in a specific limit, thereby extending previous results that were limited to a flat spacetime.

A non-canonical transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols is proposed to illustrate the conditions of thermal equilibrium in a quantum system. The proposed transformation, which alters the phase space representation of the Weyl-Wigner symbols, results in a set of quadratic equations representing the canonical equilibrium conditions. This approach enables visualization of these conditions in phase space. Furthermore, the proposed transformation facilitates a direct calculation of the canonical correlations of a quantum system in its thermal equilibrium state.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been theoretically applied across various disciplines since its inception. This concept, though initially met with skepticism, has been successfully utilized in both simulations and experiments to achieve desirable outcomes. We have witnessed the incorporation of negative absolute temperature into models and protocols within plasma physics, quantum mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, and even sports strategies. This paper explores the positive aspects of negative absolute temperature and highlights its benefits in specific contexts, presenting a more optimistic perspective on this topic.

We have developed a new electroweak symmetry breaking scenario called the easiest scoto-seesaw framework, which incorporates a specific type of neutrino mass generation known as the "neutral lepton" sector. This framework includes a specific set of dark matter properties and offers distinct predictions for Higgs boson decay patterns. Through straightforward calculations, we have determined the most critical contributions to the Higgs vacuum stability indicator, $R_{\rm vac}$, and found that the easiest scoto-seesaw scenario yields $R_{\rm vac}$ values greater than 1 at the EW scale. Furthermore, this scenario exhibits a dark matter relic density in line with WIMP predictions.

We examine the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital mixing in 4d and 5d transition metal compounds using a method that combines $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ basis sets. By adjusting the ratio of $t_{2g}$ to $e_g$ orbital amplitudes, we can mimic the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing observed in experiments and calculations. A critical mixing ratio is identified where the energy gap between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ bands reaches a minimum. Below this ratio, the $t_{2g}$ band shifts to higher energies with increasing $e_g$ amplitude, while the $e_g$ band shifts to lower energies. Above this ratio, the $t_{2g}$ band shifts to lower energies with increasing $e_g$ amplitude, while the $e_g$ band shifts to higher energies. This behavior is attributed to the competition between on-site and next-nearest neighbor Coulomb interactions. We establish that a certain variant of Floer's relative symplectic homology, defined for high-codimensional submanifolds, is invariant under certain types of symplectic transformations called rational symplectic transformations. This invariance applies specifically to a submanifold with specific boundary characteristics and certain symplectic form transformations. This result also implies the uniqueness of a particular class of closed submanifolds within symplectic transformations. This uniqueness was conjectured by McDuff. This paper further explores properties of this unique class of closed submanifolds, revealing their non-existence in even-dimensional symplectic transformations unless it equals four-dimensional transformations. This result also shows that a specific variant of Lagrangian Floer theory for closed submanifolds yields results equivalent to those obtained from relative symplectic homology for these submanifolds.

The accuracy of deep learning models for detecting health issues from chest X-rays can be significantly impaired for patients suffering from certain conditions such as COVID-19, lung cancer, and Alzheimer's disease. This problem is particularly pronounced when these models are applied in a clinical setting where patients with these conditions are being treated and assessed. Researchers have explored various methods to enhance the robustness of these models to such biases but have largely neglected the potential of modifying X-rays to counter this effect. In our work, we experiment with three approaches to artificially introduce biases in chest X-rays and investigate how they impact the models' performance. Our findings show that when image biases are introduced based on Alzheimer's disease diagnosis, the models' performance is negatively affected. To counter this, we explore three methods of modifying X-rays and find that, for Alzheimer's patients, average intensity normalization enhances the models' performance by 3.49% and 4.17% for different models. Our research into modifying X-rays to make them more representative of Alzheimer's patients is the first of its kind and paves the way for further exploration of this innovative strategy in addressing real-world clinical scenarios.

ViDaExpert is a user-friendly tool that works with complex vector data of any size to perform nonlinear reductions and in-depth analyses. This instrument, tailored for researchers working with multidimensional vector data, offers an interactive 3D visualization capability via Java. It allows for the creation of isosurface, isovolume, and streamlines based on reduced data, in addition to the generation of scatter plots from low-dimensional representations. ViDaExpert also provides a range of advanced features, including statistical analysis and nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques. This software is a valuable resource for academic professionals working in the field of vector data.
